parts.title: A Tiny Version of Earth's Northern-Light Cycle on Mars
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Mars has no single, planet-wide magnetic field like Earth's. Instead, it has patches of magnetic field stuck to its crust, and these patches are spread unevenly across the planet. Because of this, the auroras on Mars (the glowing lights in the sky, like Earth's northern lights) are complicated and change a lot. They depend both on how the planet spins and on the solar wind, the stream of charged particles that the Sun sends out.

We used measurements taken directly by the MAVEN spacecraft (short for Mars Atmospheric and Volatile EvolutioN), which recorded electrons, ions (charged atoms) and magnetic fields. With these data, we show that the auroras linked to these small crustal magnetic fields can be explained by a tiny repeating cycle. In this cycle, magnetic field lines and the charged particles (plasma) flowing along them move around in a loop. It looks like a miniature version of what happens on Earth.

On Earth, this repeating loop is called the Dungey cycle, after the scientist who discovered it. There, it works inside a single, planet-wide magnetic field shaped like a bar magnet, which is about 100 times stronger and about 20 times larger than the small crustal fields on Mars.

Seen across the whole solar system, our finding adds one more example to the collection of ideas about auroras. It helps us understand how varied the charged-particle environments of planets are, both in our own solar system and on other worlds, and how planets interact with the space around them.

Subject terms: Aurora, Magnetospheric physics (the physics of the region around a planet shaped by its magnetic field), Inner planets
parts.introduction_first:
An aurora is made when fast-moving particles hit molecules or atoms in the atmosphere. These particles must carry more than about 10 electron volts of energy, which is a tiny unit of energy used for single particles. On Earth, one of the most common kinds of aurora is called discrete aurora. It appears as bright patches of light in narrow areas around the magnetic poles, at the same places where fast electrons are falling into the atmosphere.

On Earth, these auroral electrons are sped up to tens of kilo electron volts (keV), which is tens of thousands of electron volts. They get this energy from changes in the magnetosphere, the region around a planet where the planet's own magnetic field is in charge. The magnetosphere is reshaped when the magnetic field carried by the solar wind (the interplanetary magnetic field) points partly southward. On the side of Earth facing the Sun, this incoming field joins up with Earth's own bar-magnet-shaped field, a process called magnetic reconnection. Before this, the magnetic field lines were closed, meaning both ends were attached to the planet. After reconnection, they become open, linking Earth to the solar wind.

The solar wind then carries these newly opened field lines around to the night side of the planet. There, in the long stretched-out part of the magnetosphere called the magnetotail, the field lines reconnect again and become closed once more. This repeating change, from closed to open and back to closed, is known as the Dungey cycle. It controls how plasma flows around Earth, both in the magnetosphere and in the ionosphere, the upper part of the atmosphere where air is charged.

As the newly closed loops of magnetic field relax and pull back toward Earth, electric currents flow along the field lines between the magnetosphere and the ionosphere. These currents create large electric fields that also point along the field lines, and these fields speed up electrons. The electrons then strike the atmosphere, mostly at nearly the same energy, and this makes the aurora. So auroras are the visible signs of a system of electric currents that links the solar wind, carrying its own magnetic field, to the magnetosphere and the ionosphere.
parts.introduction_rest:
Mars makes the solar wind's job a little harder. Its ionosphere can carry electric current, and its strong magnetic fields are stuck to the crust in patches that are spread unevenly and turn along with the planet.

If we look only at the plasma, the region around Mars looks, in the first rough approximation, like the region around Venus. There, the solar wind's magnetic field simply wraps around the planet's ionosphere, like a sheet of fabric being pulled over a head. This is called a draping. But Mars has its own magnetic fields, stuck to the crust in particular places, and these change the picture a great deal.

Three missions have seen auroras on Mars: the Mars Express mission, the MAVEN mission and the Emirates Mars Hope Mission. They found two kinds. Diffuse auroras are spread out and fairly shapeless. Discrete auroras are bright patches in narrow areas.

Earlier studies of MAVEN's aurora data looked at where these auroras and their electrons appear. They found that the auroras tend to happen over the strongest crustal fields in the southern hemisphere. They also tend to happen when the solar wind's magnetic field points partly southward, which scientists write as IMF − BY. And they differ between dusk and dawn, the local times on the planet.

Scientists think the southward pointing helps because it makes magnetic reconnection easier. The crustal fields can reconnect with the solar wind's magnetic field in the magnetosheath, the layer of solar wind that has been slowed and squeezed as it hit the planet. This reconnection changes the crustal field lines from closed to open, so electrons from outside can reach the atmosphere.

These findings suggest that magnetic reconnection is important for making the discrete auroras. But they tell us little about how the auroral electrons actually get their energy. Magnetic reconnection itself gives electrons very little energy on Mars, because the Alfven speed there is very small, only tens of kilometres per second. The Alfven speed is the speed at which a magnetic field pushes on the plasma around it.

In this paper, we look closely at one case from MAVEN's measurements, taken on 25 February 2017. In it, we show a tiny Dungey cycle on Mars. We describe how reconnection between the solar wind's magnetic field and the crustal fields, happening in particular places, controls how much magnetic field lines pass through the crustal regions and how the plasma moves around them. We show that the way the electrons for the discrete auroras get their energy is a natural part of this cycle.

To do this, we take a well-established way of thinking about Earth and apply it to the complicated crustal magnetic regions of Mars, at a scale 20 times smaller. This way of thinking has five parts: magnetic reconnection, electric currents flowing along the magnetic field lines, the speeding up of electrons, the movement of plasma in the ionosphere, and the aurora itself. Earlier research has studied four of these, mostly one at a time. Our study presents the fifth, the movement of plasma in the ionosphere. This is hard to measure, because it is at the very limit of what the ion instrument can do.

Our case study gives measurements of three of these parts at the same time: the electric currents along the field lines, the speeding up of electrons, and the movement of plasma in the ionosphere. It also shows that the directions these three parts point in agree with theory. Our study offers a way of thinking that links all five parts into one consistent physical picture of the Martian aurora, and this picture applies to all earlier research on the topic. We give several more examples to show that it works in general.
parts.methods:
## Methods

### Observations

We used data from the MAVEN spacecraft, which carried three instruments that measured the charged particles and the magnetic field around Mars. The first, the Solar Wind Electron Analyzer (SWEA), measured electrons. The second, the Magnetometer (MAG), measured the magnetic field. The third, the suprathermal and thermal ion composition instrument (STATIC), measured ions.

The SWEA instrument could measure electrons with energies from 3 to 4600 electron volts. It sorted them into 64 energy steps, and each step covered a range of 16.7% of the energy (written ΔE/E = 16.7%). The instrument looked across a wide slice of space, 360° around and 120° up and down, and it could tell apart directions 22.5° apart in one direction and 7° apart in the other. It took a measurement every 2 to 4 seconds.

The STATIC instrument measured ions with energies from 0.1 electron volts up to 30 keV (30,000 electron volts). Its energy steps were 16% of the energy (ΔE/E = 16%). It looked across about 360° around and 90° up and down, and it could tell apart directions 22.5° apart in one direction and 6° apart in the other. It took a measurement every 4 seconds.

STATIC also worked out how heavy each ion was by timing how long it took to fly through the instrument, a method called time-of-flight. This let it tell apart the main kinds of ions found at Mars. Each kind is identified by its mass divided by its electric charge (written m/q). Hydrogen ions (H+) have a value of 1, and H2+ and He++ have a value of 2. Oxygen ions (O+) have a value of 16, O2+ a value of 32, and CO2+ a value of 44.

The magnetometer measured the magnetic field in all three directions. It was accurate to about 0.1 nanotesla (nT), a unit of magnetic field strength, and it could measure fields from −65536 to +65536 nT. It took a measurement every 1/32 of a second.
parts.results:
## Results

### What MAVEN measured

Figure 1 shows what MAVEN measured from 22:17 to 22:22 on 25 February 2017. We give times in universal time (UT), which is the standard time used by scientists around the world. More detailed measurements are in Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2.

The measurements were taken at about 20:00 local time, which is roughly 8 pm on the Martian side of the planet. At that hour the Sun was about 100° below the horizon, so the spacecraft was near the dusk terminator, the line where day turns into night. The measurements also came from the area with the strongest crustal magnetic fields, which is part of the path the spacecraft followed (shown in Fig. 1e).

In Fig. 1c, the number of electrons arriving at the spacecraft (the electron flux) was much higher than at other times, during two separate stretches. This was especially true for the most energetic electrons. The energies at which the flux peaked were spread out over time. This suggests that these electrons had been sped up along the magnetic field lines, much like the electrons that make Earth's discrete auroras.

**Fig. 1. The MAVEN measurements of the tiny Dungey-like cycle.**

Measurements from MAVEN on 25 February 2017: a the change in the magnetic field, Br, in the local horizontal plane; b the current flowing along the magnetic field lines, worked out from the change in the magnetic field (j//b, blue) and from the fast electrons (j//e, orange); c the energies of the fast electrons, shown as the energy flux reaching the spacecraft (in units of eV cm−2 sr−1 s−1 eV−1); and d the speed of the O2+ ions (V(O2+)) in the local horizontal plane. e The current along the field lines (j//b), the east-west part of the O2+ speed (where it is above 1 km/s), and the times when fast electrons were seen (j//e above 0.1 μA/m2, shown as orange dots). These are laid over a color map of the modeled crustal magnetic field pointing straight up or down at 250 km above the surface. A positive j//b means current flowing upward across the local horizontal plane, and a negative j//b means current flowing downward. This is true whether the local magnetic field points up or down.

We used a rule, based on earlier measurements, that links how much energy the electrons carry to how brightly they make the sky glow. By this rule, these energized electrons could make a kind of aurora in the upper atmosphere of Mars. It is called the CO Cameron band, a particular set of ultraviolet light given off by carbon monoxide molecules. Seen from the side of the planet, it would be about 10 kilo-Reighley (kR) bright. This is similar to some of the brightest auroras that MAVEN's Imaging UltraViolet Spectrograph (IUVS) instrument has seen.

In fact, IUVS did see a CO Cameron band at 22:18:37 to 22:19:30 UT on 25 February 2017, with a brightness of 0.6 to 1.4 kR. This was close to the time we studied, but it happened at a different place: at latitudes [−39.9°, −36.7°] and longitudes [182.5°, 183.0°], not where we measured the electrons. We estimated that the auroral electrons at 22:18:20, the moment closest to the IUVS measurements, would make the sky 4–6 kR bright. That is a few times brighter than what IUVS measured. So the electrons in this case study carry enough energy to make an aurora that IUVS could see. The two brightnesses probably differ because the electrons changed over time and because the two measurements came from different places.

Near the energized electrons, the measured magnetic field was not the same as the local crustal field. The change in the magnetic field, Br, from the crustal field (Fig. 1a) pointed mainly east or west. This fits with a sheet of current flowing along the field lines in an east-west direction. We call this kind of current a field-aligned current (FAC).

We assumed this, and we also know that the spacecraft was moving mainly from north to south (Fig. 1e). From these two facts we worked out the current along the field lines, j//b, from the change in the magnetic field, BEWr. It is the blue line in Fig. 1b. A positive j//b means current flowing upward across the local horizontal plane, and a negative j//b means current flowing downward. This is true whether the local magnetic field points up or down. The uncertainty in j//b is about 7%, shown in Supplementary Figs. S1f, S3f and S4f. The Supplementary Information explains in detail how we calculated the uncertainty in j//b and the other key measurements.

Comparing Fig. 1b and 1c, the energized electrons mostly went along with upward current. In both time periods, the upward current was sandwiched between two downward currents.

We can also work out the current carried by the electrons themselves, j//e, from the number of electrons we measured. It is the orange line in Fig. 1b, and its uncertainty is about 15%, also shown in Supplementary Figs. S1f, S3f and S4f. Where the current was upward (j//b above 0), j//e agreed reasonably well with j//b. This happened from 22:18:15 to 22:18:28 UT and from 22:21:06 to 22:21:35 UT. This supports the idea that the upward current is carried by energized electrons falling toward the planet.

When the current was downward (j//b below 0), from 22:17:55 to 22:18:15 UT and from 22:21:35 to 22:21:50 UT, j//e was close to 0. This is what we would expect. A downward current should be carried by electrons rising up from the ionosphere, which are more plentiful there, so we would not expect electrons to be sped up downward.

At two particular moments, about 22:18:30 UT and 22:21:05 UT, j//e was above 0 while j//b was below 0, even though we expected j//e to be close to zero. At those times, j//b (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Figs. S3 and S4) changed quickly in size and direction, within less than 1 second. This points to fast changes in time, in place, or both, that MAVEN's electron measurements could not capture, because it took a measurement every 2 seconds.

Besides the main case study above, we found six more events, shown in Supplementary Figs. S5–S10. In most of them, j//e agreed reasonably well with j//b when j//b was above 0. The exceptions were when j//b changed in less than 2 seconds, which was too fast for the electron measurements to follow.

Finally, Fig. 1d shows that the overall speeds of two kinds of ions, O2+ (solid line) and O+ (dashed line), in the local plane were very similar. The error bars in Fig. 1d show the uncertainty in each speed, and they are also shown in Supplementary Figs. S1j, S3j and S4j. Near the energized electrons, both kinds of ions had a strong east-west speed (VEW(O2+) and VEW(O+)). This suggests that the overall flow of the ionosphere is east or west. In particular, the east-west flow switched direction at 22:18 to 22:19 UT. The Supplementary Information gives more detailed measurements and explains how we worked out Br, j//b and j//e.

### The tiny Dungey-like cycle on Mars

Figure 1e brings all these key measurements together. It shows the current along the field lines, j//b, as magenta lines when it is upward and cyan lines when it is downward. It shows the auroral electrons, where j//e is larger than 0.1 μA/m2, as orange dots. It also shows the east-west speed of O2+, where it is larger than 1 km/s, as black arrows. All of these are laid over a map of the crustal magnetic field. Together, they can be explained by a tiny Dungey-like cycle, in which magnetic reconnection and the flow of magnetic field and plasma move around in a loop, as shown in Fig. 2.

**Fig. 2. How the tiny Dungey cycle works on Mars.**

a The starting conditions for the first magnetic reconnection, where the closed crustal magnetic fields meet the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF, labeled BY) that has been bent around the planet at the dusk terminator. The yellow and gray shaded areas are the day side and the night side. The blue and red shaded areas are crustal magnetic fields: blue where the field points inward (Br below 0) and red where it points outward (Br above 0). b How the pattern of magnetic field lines changes, and how the magnetic field lines move around, in the tiny Dungey cycle. c A close-up of the matching flow of plasma and currents in the ionosphere, with the numbered circles marking where the numbered field lines in (b) touch the ionosphere. None of the drawings is to scale.

Figure 2a sketches the starting conditions. The crustal fields lie near the dusk terminator. Before and after the time we studied, the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) carried by the solar wind pointed mainly in the Bx direction, with Bx above 0, and in the By direction, with By below 0. This is the IMF direction that favors auroras. As the solar wind pushes past the planet, it swaps some of its motion with the planet's ions. This tilts the bent IMF southward in the southern hemisphere. That tilt sets it up well for magnetic reconnection with the local crustal fields, which have a northward part in the horizontal plane (the upper arcade).

Figure 2b shows the sequence of changes in the pattern of magnetic field lines that fits the tiny Dungey-like cycle. It begins with the first magnetic reconnection between the bent IMF and the upper arcade. This splits the closed field line (1) into two open field lines, labeled 2 and 2′. The solar wind then carries these open field lines further down the magnetotail. There, the second magnetic reconnection happens between the open field lines (3 and 3′), which point in opposite directions. This creates new closed field lines (4). These new closed field lines relax and are then carried toward Mars (5 and 6), which completes the Dungey-like cycle.

As the magnetic field lines move around in this loop, the points where they touch the ionosphere (their footpoints) are carried along by the flows of plasma in the ionosphere, just as on Earth. As Fig. 2c shows, the flow most likely goes clockwise in the upper crustal patch and counterclockwise in the lower crustal patch. This way, the closed loops carried toward Mars (4→5→6) sit toward the center. Underneath them are closed crustal loops that have not been opened, and the open field lines lie outside the closed loops.

These ionospheric flows are driven by the E × B drift, the motion of charged particles across a magnetic field when an electric field is present. Given the direction of the local magnetic fields, a set of electric fields E that point inward is needed to create these flows in both crustal patches. The real flows do not necessarily stretch across tens of degrees of longitude. They could be much smaller than drawn, depending on the pattern of the crustal field.

The tiny Dungey-like cycle we show here looks like half of the Dungey cycle on Earth's dusk side. The two crustal patches where the Martian ionospheric flows happen would match the dusk halves of Earth's northern and southern polar regions, as shown in Fig. 3b–d.

**Fig. 3. Drawings of three kinds of plasma and magnetic field cycles.**

a The Vasyliunas cycle, which works on giant planets such as Jupiter and Saturn. b The Dungey cycle, which works on planets with a strong magnetic field such as Earth and Mercury. c The tiny Dungey-like cycle on Mars, from this study. d The flow pattern of the Dungey cycle, seen from the north and from the south. e The flow pattern of the tiny Dungey-like cycle from this study. None of the drawings is to scale. IMF is the interplanetary magnetic field.

The inward-pointing electric fields set up pairs of currents that cross the magnetic field lines in the ionosphere. These currents close by flowing along the field lines between the ionosphere and the magnetosphere. Currents flowing away from the ionosphere are carried mainly by electrons falling into the atmosphere. If there are not enough of these electrons to carry the current, large electric fields that point along the field lines could form. These are called double layers. They would speed up electrons toward the planet until the electrons all have nearly the same energy, so that they can carry the current needed. These electrons then make discrete auroras.

The MAVEN measurements shown here contain the key parts of this process, as highlighted in Fig. 1e. In both crustal patches, the current flows downward, then upward, then downward again (Fig. 2c). This matches the j//b we worked out in Fig. 1b, e. The energized electrons also mostly appeared at the same times as the upward current (j//b above 0) (Fig. 1b, e). The current carried by these energized electrons, j//e, agreed reasonably well with the upward current, j//b. These links support the idea that electrons are sped up to carry the current needed.

In addition, a strong east or west flow of plasma was seen mostly between the downward and upward currents (Fig. 1d, e). Near the dusk terminator, east is the same as tailward, away from the Sun, and west is the same as sunward. This fits the flow pattern drawn in Fig. 2c.

Besides the main case study, Fig. 4 shows the current, the flow speed and the energized electrons for all 7 events we found, placed on a map of the planet. These extra events (Events 1, 3–7) look like the main case study (Event 2), and they happened at many different latitudes and longitudes. Events 4 and 6 happened at almost the same place and at the same local time, even though they were seen 11 days apart.

Most of the events happened at latitudes [−40°, −55°] after dusk. Event 3, however, happened farther south, with the crustal field pointing the opposite way, before dawn (local time 04). This fits earlier findings that auroras differ between dawn and dusk. The events happened in different crustal fields, or at the same place at different times. This suggests that the tiny Dungey-like cycle runs regularly in these small magnetospheres.

**Fig. 4. All the MAVEN events, shown on a map of the planet.**

For each event, the current along the field lines (j//b), the east-west speed of O2+ (where it is above 1 km/s), and the energized electrons (j//e above 0.1 μA/m2, shown as orange dots) are laid over a color map of the modeled crustal magnetic field pointing straight up or down at 250 km above the surface. The date, hour in UT and local time (LT) of each MAVEN measurement are listed in the lower right corner. The numbers in brackets are the event numbers, and a and b refer to the two parts of the same event.
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

Comparing Mars with Earth is one of the main goals of planetary science. So it is worth asking how big and how fast this tiny Dungey-like cycle is on Mars, compared with the one on Earth. For this discussion we use the values from our main case study.

On Earth, the second reconnection, in the magnetotail, happens about 15 Earth radii down the tail. (An Earth radius is the distance from the center of Earth to its surface.) Mars's crustal fields are much smaller. Earth's bar-magnet-shaped field stretches from one pole to the other, a distance of 2 Earth radii. Mars's crustal field "dipole" (a single patch of crustal field) is only 1000 km across. If we scale Earth's distance down to fit Mars, we would expect the second reconnection on Mars to happen a few Mars radii downstream, roughly 7500 km.

The solar wind is slowed down as it hits the planet, and it then carries the open field lines downstream at about 100 km/s. At that speed, the whole cycle on Mars takes about 1 minute. On Earth it takes about 1 hour, and on Mercury it is about the same as the cycle period there.

In the ionosphere, the plasma flows at about 2 km/s on Mars, which is similar to Earth. The local magnetic field is about 270 nT (nano tesla, a unit of magnetic field strength). From these two numbers we can work out the electric field that pushes the plasma across the magnetic field lines. It is 0.5 mV/m (millivolts per metre).

In our case study, the system of currents stretches about 3° in latitude, which is about 200 km. The currents flow along the field lines, some downward and some upward, in pairs. The voltage between each downward and upward pair (over a distance of 100 km) would be roughly 50 V. That is about 3 orders of magnitude (roughly 1000 times) smaller than the voltage across Earth's polar caps during quiet times, which is tens of kV (thousands of volts). The distance over which this voltage changes is smaller by one order of magnitude (10 times), and the local magnetic field is smaller by two orders of magnitude (100 times).

The cycle lasts about 2.5 minutes, so one half of it lasts about 75 seconds. From this we can infer that the loop of plasma flow in the ionosphere is 300 km long, or about 7° at a latitude of −45°.

We can also estimate how much power this cycle uses up in the ionosphere. First, we estimate the Pedersen conductivity at the footpoints of the field lines, the places where the field lines reach the ionosphere. Pedersen conductivity (σP) describes how easily electric current flows across the magnetic field lines in the ionosphere. We estimate it to be 5 × 10−3 S/m (siemens per metre, the unit of conductivity). It is highest at an altitude of about 180 km.

To get this value, we used the MAVEN measurements for that day. The density of neutral CO2 (carbon dioxide) was 108 cm−3, and the density of O2+ (oxygen ions) was 104 cm−3. We also used a magnetic field strength of 500 nT. We scaled this from a bar-magnet-shaped field placed at the surface, where the field strength (|B|) falls off with height as 1/z2.

We assume the electric field across the field lines is the same at the footpoints (E⊥ = 0.5 mV/m). Then the current density across the field lines (J⊥), meaning the amount of current flowing through each square metre, is 2.5 μA/m2 (microamperes per square metre). We calculate it as

(1) J⊥ = σP E⊥,

which matches the density of currents along the field lines that has been observed.

This gives a local rate of energy loss of J⊥ ⋅ E⊥ = 10−9 W/m3 (watts per cubic metre). Over the whole region, the total power loss P is 106 W (one million watts). We calculate it as

(2) P = J⊥ ⋅ E⊥ V,

where V is the volume in which the energy is lost. We take this volume to be 20 km tall (2 neutral scale heights, a measure of how quickly the density of the atmosphere drops with height), 200 km in latitude and 300 km in longitude.

It is also worth noting that another instrument has seen more kinds of aurora than MAVEN's IUVS instrument (the Imaging Ultraviolet Spectrometer). This is the Emirates Ultraviolet Spectrometer (EMUS), carried by the Emirates Hope Mars Mission (EMM). EMUS has seen auroras not only where the crustal fields are strong but also where the magnetic field is weak.

EMUS is much more sensitive than IUVS. Because of this, EMUS can detect much fainter auroras. These come from solar wind electrons falling into the atmosphere, and from photoelectrons, which are electrons knocked loose from the ionosphere by sunlight. IUVS mostly detects auroras from electrons that have been sped up to much higher energies, and these carry far more energy. IUVS's aurora detections are mostly limited to places with moderate or strong crustal fields. This suggests that these auroras are set off by electrons that are probably sped up (and arrive in larger numbers) by processes linked to strong crustal fields.

There is another piece of supporting evidence. EMUS sees auroras about 10–30% of the time, except in crustal field regions that are permanently closed. That is similar to how often magnetic field lines let solar wind electrons or photoelectrons fall into the atmosphere on the night side. IUVS, by contrast, sees auroras only about 0.1% to a few percent of the time. This suggests that the auroras EMUS detects come from electron populations that are common, while the auroras IUVS detects come from comparatively rare electron populations, such as those sped up by voltages along the field lines.

Our results help explain how discrete auroras link the solar wind, the magnetosphere and the ionosphere on a planet. In particular, they show the basic roles that three things play in closing the loop of electric currents: the speeding up of auroral electrons, magnetic reconnection, and the circulation of magnetic field lines and plasma.

On Earth, this circulation is driven by the interaction between the southward magnetic field carried by the solar wind and the planet's global bar-magnet-shaped field. This is the Dungey cycle. Saturn and Jupiter also have global bar-magnet-shaped fields. On these giant planets, however, a different circulation, called the Vasyliunas cycle, plays a bigger part. It is linked to the fact that these planets have their own sources of plasma inside them, which makes the plasma's tendency to spin along with the planet take over the reconnection in the magnetotail, as shown in Fig. 3a.

It is therefore worth pointing out that, in Mars's tiny magnetospheres, our study shows a picture more like Earth's, including the role of auroral electrons in closing the loop of currents. Apart from its size, described above, the Martian case shares several features with Earth's Dungey cycle. However, only half of the crustal field "dipole" is exposed to the solar wind, and the other half is buried under the surface. This cycle should also run regularly in a similar way over the planet's many sources of crustal magnetic field, as Mars rotates and as conditions in the solar wind change.

This tiny Dungey-like cycle is therefore a third type of cycle in the solar system. It links a planet's magnetic field lines and plasma with the solar wind, and it comes with its own discrete auroras. It adds to what we know about how varied the charged-particle environments of planets are, both in our own solar system and on other worlds. It also improves our ability to use auroras, seen from a distance, to learn about a planet's magnetic field.
